narrative: Four feature requests over 18 months, all delivered and met with positive follow-up ('really pleased with how it turned out'). No complaints, no recurring faults, no competitor talk. An engaged account building on the product, not one showing any risk signal.

Three routine technical tickets (a connector sync gap, an alert routing miss, a re-authentication question) all resolved within days with no recurrence or complaint. Nothing beyond ordinary product friction.

competitor_mentions.quote: As part of our January tooling review we looked briefly at Storsund BI, though nothing's decided

narrative: Three tickets across five months show the quiet pattern to watch for: a report builder crash led the team to start 'saving more frequently and keeping a local backup of the layout as a precaution', and unreliable budget alerts led them to add 'a manual weekly check as a backstop' rather than trust the fix. The same ticket casually mentions a January look at Storsund BI. Tone stays polite throughout, but two separate reliability problems have been worked around rather than resolved, which is the accumulation pattern that precedes quiet churn more than any loud complaint would.
Two unrelated, well-spaced tickets (a formula bug, an ownership-transfer question), both resolved quickly with no follow-up complaint. No pattern of risk here.

competitor_mentions.quote: Someone on the team mentioned Storsund BI as an alternative during a demo we sat in on last month, so it would be good to get this looking solid again.
Someone mentioned Dashlume claims near-real-time alerting, so curious what the expected delay is meant to be here.

narrative: Seven tickets over six months cover a range of one-off bugs (API timeout, a blank dashboard tile, a delayed alert, a missing API field), each resolved within days with no recurrence. Two competitor names surface only in passing, tied to a demo and a documentation curiosity rather than any evaluation. Busy with variety but not deteriorating.

Nine tickets over a year, mostly feature requests and minor UI bugs, resolved fast (often 1-4 days) with consistently appreciative closings ('Appreciated', 'thanks', 'Quick one hopefully'). A highly engaged, satisfied account with no unresolved threads.

VP Finance Sigrid Jokinen's account trends downward: a Salesforce connector outage ran two and a half weeks before resolution ('I've tried everything suggested in your documentation. Please escalate if needed'), and five months later a dashboard slowdown is reported as 'not workable for daily use' and left open with no further ticket. Ending on an unresolved, frustrated complaint from a senior stakeholder is a meaningful signal given how few tickets this account has raised.
Three routine access and configuration tickets over six months (auditor access twice, an alert display mix-up), all resolved without complaint. Healthy, low-touch account.

Five tickets show the quiet-attrition pattern the guidance warns about: alerts arriving hours late pushed the team 'back to checking figures manually in Excel each afternoon rather than relying on the alerts', and a follow-up ticket confirms 'the fix doesn't seem to have held' while explicitly deprioritising it: 'no immediate pressure to resolve this quickly. Wanted to keep it on record.' Export formatting breakage gets the same resignation ('We can live with reformatting manually for now'). Two core modules are being quietly worked around rather than fixed, and the customer has stopped expecting a real resolution.
Three routine tickets (template sharing, a connector question, export access) spaced widely apart, all resolved without complaint. No concerning pattern.

A rough first year, in which exports, API timeouts and dashboard reconciliation each recurred and culminated in 'we've raised six tickets since summer on essentially three recurring problems... I'd like to talk to someone above first-line support', was followed by a genuine turnaround. Five straight months of calm, appreciative tickets followed an April call: 'Things have been much more stable since our call in April, thank you', 'the export scheduler has been rock solid since the update in June', 'Dashboards have been reliable for months now, appreciated.' This is the escalation-then-resolution arc that reads as healthy, not at risk.

competitor_mentions.quote: We've begun quietly benchmarking Storsund BI's API alongside this as part of general due diligence, mostly because we'd like to understand whether this kind of slowdown is a one-off or a pattern worth planning around.

narrative: API response times degraded from around 4 to 12-15 minutes in March, and in the same ticket the customer disclosed active due-diligence benchmarking of a competitor's API — a serious signal, not a casual aside. A May follow-up confirms the issue 'never really returned to normal' and that the team adjusted its own job scheduling to absorb the delay rather than push for a real fix ('no need to prioritise this above other things'). Active competitor benchmarking plus a quietly-accepted, unresolved defect is a meaningful risk combination despite the calm tone.
Two unrelated, well-spaced informational tickets a year apart, both resolved without incident. Sparse but neutral traffic, consistent with a healthy low-touch account.

Two routine configuration questions were followed by an alert failing to trigger despite the threshold being 'clearly breached', left open with no further ticket. Volume is too low to establish a firm pattern, but ending on an unresolved, factual complaint is worth a watch on an otherwise quiet account.

A difficult year — duplicate alerts, a dashboard freeze recurring three times ('Third issue in three months. Getting hard to explain to my manager', later 'is anyone actually looking at this account?') and an explicit request to escalate beyond first-line support — was followed by a confirmed turnaround: fixes held across multiple tickets afterward ('report builder has been stable, no crashes on the calculated columns', 'Confirming alerts haven't duplicated since the changes went in', 'saved a lot of duplicated work across the team, appreciated'). Like the other escalation-recovery account in this batch, this reads as genuine resolution rather than lingering risk.

VP Finance Aino Lund's account cycles through four chronic faults — weekly report delivery, connector reliability, alert firing, and API stability — each marked resolved and each recurring, culminating in 'this is the longest outage yet' (20 days) and 'Connector has failed again. Third time this year... I want this escalated. 25 days is too long and I should not have to follow up repeatedly to get a resolution.' Unlike the two escalation-recovery accounts in this batch, there is no confirming ticket of sustained stability afterward — the final entries are still about connector delays and re-verifying whether settings held. This is the most severe pattern in the batch: high volume, no durable resolution, explicit escalation demands from a VP.
Six well-spaced tickets over 13 months, a mix of routine questions and feature requests, all resolved and none recurring. Consistently healthy, low-friction account.

Six tickets over four months show the quiet pattern: intermittent API 500 errors and a connector silently dropping rows both persisted past their fixes ('it happened again on Monday's run, same pattern'), pushing the team to build 'a standing manual export as a cross-check' and to start pulling data 'straight into Excel... rather than trusting the connector output'. By September the customer is explicitly deprioritising a third recurring issue (alerts occasionally not firing): 'given everything else we've flagged this year... we're not chasing this one hard.' Calm tone throughout, but three separate reliability problems have been quietly worked around rather than fixed.
Four sparse, well-spaced feature requests and questions over eight months, all resolved without complaint. Healthy, low-touch account.

Head of Operations Sanna Strand's account shows a chronic, worsening export fault: the same failure recurs three times with resolution time climbing from 4 to 7 to 10 days, prompting an explicit demand to 'speak with someone at a senior technical level, not just receive a "please try again" response.' The final ticket, a 16-day API problem on the exports-trigger endpoint, closes with the customer's own unaddressed suspicion of 'a broader issue with the exports infrastructure.' Resolution times trending the wrong direction on a repeated fault, plus an unresolved suspicion at the very end, is a clear watch signal.
